evidence.claim: Designated a Utah State Scenic Byway in 1990, the route is promoted by the Forest Service for its roadside double waterfall, reservoir recreation and passage into Heber Valley.
evidence.quote: (6) Provo Canyon Scenic Byway. US Route 189, beginning at SR-52, and running to SR-113, near Charleston; and State Route 113, from US-189 running to US-40 in Heber City. (a) Designated April 9, 1990.

evidence.claim: Before the road, the canyon connected Timpanogos Utes in Utah Valley and the Uinta Basin.
evidence.quote: The Timpanogos Utes resided in both Utah Valley and the Uinta Basin; therefore, Provo Canyon provided an essential connection

evidence.claim: Utah Valley settlers pressed for a road into Heber Valley, and construction in 1858 made settlement easier.
evidence.quote: Settlers of Utah Valley pushed the territorial government to create a road up the Provo Canyon

evidence.claim: The road was paved in the early 1930s and widened from two lanes to four by 1992.
evidence.quote: The road was first paved in the early 1930s, and In 1992, the expansion of US-189 from two lanes to four lanes was completed.

evidence.claim: The scenic byway’s course changed again in 2003, moving from eastern US 189 onto SR-113.
evidence.quote: Realigned onto SR-113 from the eastern portion of US-189 February 25, 2003.

evidence.claim: Starting at SR-52 on US 189, follow the river up the canyon, past Bridal Veil Falls and toward Deer Creek Reservoir at its upper end.
evidence.quote: US Route 189, beginning at SR-52, and running to SR-113, near Charleston

evidence.claim: Near Charleston, the designated route turns onto SR-113, continuing through Midway and ending at US 40 in Heber City.
evidence.quote: US Route 189, beginning at SR-52, and running to SR-113, near Charleston; and State Route 113, from US-189 running to US-40 in Heber City.

evidence.claim: The reservoir’s open water and Midway’s town square give the journey different stopping points beyond the canyon walls.

flags: Waterfall height conflicts: the canyon article gives 617 feet; the falls article gives 607. Omitted the number.

The canyon article conflates railroad companies and skips earlier tourist operations. The railroad article also describes a partial closure beginning in 2022 without clearly establishing reopening to Vivian Park. Dropped the current claim of excursion service all the way to Vivian Park.
Dam construction completed in 1941 is distinguished from the broader project’s 1955 completion in the park article.
Winter closure practical note was checked against the cache only, using the required 2026-10-11 date; it is a recurring condition, not a claim of a current closure.
Indigenous route history is supported only by the saved secondary canyon account; no tribal-authored source is cached.
